Estimate which month the snapshot describes. Use only the figures supplied plus your general knowledge of economic history.

Reply with one JSON object and nothing else:
{"year": yyyy, "month": m, "confidence": c, "cues": ["...", "..."]}
Rules: year is an integer from 2007 to 2026; month is an integer from 1 to 12; c in [0, 1] is your confidence that the guess is within 6 months of the truth; 1 to 3 short cues citing the inputs.
text:
The snapshot looks like mid-to-late 2023. Several figures point there:

- The fed funds rate is 5.07%, which fits the period after the July 2023 hike.
- Core CPI is 5.33% year over year, and headline CPI is 4.13%, down 4.37 points over 12 months. Headline CPI was about 9% in mid-2022, so it was falling fast.
- The 10y-2y spread is -1.02, which fits mid-2023.
- The 2-year yield is 4.87%, and the 10-year yield is 3.85%, up 0.37 over 3 months. The 10-year was around 3.8% in early June 2023, and it was about 4.1% at the end of July.
- Headline CPI of 4.13% year over year matches May 2023 (4.0%) or April (4.9%). June 2023 was 3.0%, so the CPI reading is closest to May. Core CPI in May was 5.3%, which also matches.
- Unemployment of 3.7% matches May 2023 (3.7%), though it was 3.6% in June. Payrolls averaged about 283k over 3 months, which fits March-May 2023 once revisions are included.
- The VIX is 13.54, which fits the end of May or June 2023 (June ended near 13.6).
- US large-cap equity returned +6.5% over 1 month, which matches June 2023 (S&P up about 6.5%). The 3-month return of +10.2% also fits June.
- The 10-year yield at the end of June 2023 was about 3.84%. The 2-year was 4.87%. Both match June.

So the end of June 2023 fits best. The CPI and unemployment figures are the latest published values, so they would still be May data at that point.
